hero.headline: Beetlejuice the musical closes final performances this weekend at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, featuring actor Ryan Stajmiger in the iconic striped suit.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical is now playing at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7. The Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film.

The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble. Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. Very early in the run, he experienced one unexpected moment when a wig change on stage went wrong. The second wig came off with the first wig, so he was bald for an entire scene.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres, now 99% contained after rekindling Saturday
cards.teaser: A brush fire in Indiantown that began Friday afternoon escalated significantly over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Mart.
cards.body:
A brush fire in Indiantown that began Friday afternoon escalated significantly over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service. The fire started Friday, June 5, when MCFR firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened at the time.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to the same general area to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from MCFR, the Florida Forest Service, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The Florida Forest Service established plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, and MCFR's drone team identified remaining hotspots.

Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area, though officials confirmed there was no broader threat to the public. Residents were advised to expect smoky conditions throughout the weekend as suppression efforts continued. Officials noted that early indications suggested the fire may have been a holdover fire, meaning a lightning strike could have smoldered underground for days before igniting visible flames.

The fire reached approximately 125 acres in total size and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. The Florida Forest Service remains in the area monitoring conditions to ensure no further flare-ups occur. The investigation into the fire's origin remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat Jared Moskowitz Team Up to Urge Floridians to Prepare for Hurricane Season
cards.body:
Republicans and Democrats Unite on Hurricane Preparedness

Florida's hurricane season runs through November, and two congressmen are putting aside partisan differences to encourage residents to get ready. Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican from Congressional District 19 in Southwest Florida, and Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat from Congressional District 23 in Southeast Florida, have created a public service announcement to help Floridians prepare for potential storms. The effort demonstrates that disaster preparedness is a concern that unites people across political lines.

Both lawmakers emphasized that hurricanes pose risks to all Floridians regardless of their political affiliation. "Protecting Florida communities is a shared duty that transcends any political divide," Donalds said, adding that the safety of all Floridians must come first. He encouraged residents to take steps now rather than waiting for a storm to approach. Moskowitz reinforced this message, stating that hurricanes do not discriminate based on party affiliation. "Hurricanes don't care whether you're a Democrat or a Republican; they hit everyone," Moskowitz said. He stressed the importance of beginning preparations immediately instead of waiting until a storm appears on the radar.

The congressmen have outlined specific preparation steps for residents to follow. Floridians should assemble a disaster supply kit containing at least seven days of supplies as soon as possible. Residents need to identify their evacuation zones and understand the distinction between hurricane watches and warnings. Pet owners should develop plans for their animals during emergencies, and business owners should establish emergency procedures for their operations during storm events. Both lawmakers also recommend downloading mobile applications from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to stay informed and connected during hurricane season.

This bipartisan initiative comes as Florida enters an active portion of hurricane season. Donalds is currently running for Florida Governor in this year's elections. Moskowitz announced his candidacy in late May for Florida's 25th House seat, adjusting his campaign focus after the Florida Legislature finalized new redistricting congressional maps in the spring. Despite their different political parties and campaign goals, both representatives have prioritized public safety by working together on this important messaging campaign.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County parents, commissioner respond to teen takeover trend at Wellington mall
cards.teaser: A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting an increased law enforcement presence from the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase law enforcement presence at the mall. Teen takeovers are large gatherings of teens at malls, beaches or parks that typically devolve into violence. The trend has been spreading across Florida, including an event in Clearwater at the end of May that resulted in widespread property damage, fights and the shooting of a 17-year-old. Shoppers at the Wellington Green Mall on Friday noticed the heightened law enforcement presence. Savanna Restrepo, who was there picking up her son Isaac from summer camp, said the visible police presence was reassuring. Fellow parent Eric Delgado said the response was the right call, stating "We need a strong police presence." Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier took to social media to call the events "unacceptable" and announced a plan to "investigate and prosecute those who are responsible for these events."

Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss said community safety is a priority but pointed to a root cause, noting that kids need something to do. Weiss said parents should take steps to fill that time with activities at community rec centers throughout the county and cities. He acknowledged that summer camp costs can be a barrier for some families and noted that Palm Beach County offers scholarship opportunities for summer camps. Weiss emphasized that the bottom line is parental involvement, urging parents to know what their kids are doing and stay in contact with them.

cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators fight federal feeding ban proposed for waters off state's coast
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from shark diving industry operators who warn it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry, with operators warning it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses while doing little to curb safety risks. H.R. 3831, also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. A coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible encounters with sharks, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has yet asked operators to present data or explain their practices.

Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives. They argue this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent. However, Florida operators and some researchers say the Hawaii experience tells a different story. Since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported, and according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration in Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
cards.body:
35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. ChildNet supports foster kids and young men and women through education, adoptions and independent living resources. Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward.

Diaz said, "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard." Saintfort echoed that sentiment, saying, "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff." Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the significance of the evening: "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them!" Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club at community center
cards.teaser: Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, has launched a new juniors chess club to share his love of the game with his community.
cards.body:
Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, launched a new juniors chess club after developing a passion for the game at age 5 while playing with family. Baptiste wanted to share his love of chess with his community and encourage kids to respect board games. "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff," Baptiste said. "I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games."

More than 36 juniors have already joined the Atlantis Chess Club at the Port St. Lucie Community Center, where it meets every Friday. The club attracts players of all skill levels and will soon begin two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, said the club aims to develop young leaders. "It will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making," Kempton said.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block fundraiser in West Palm Beach supports Transpire Help LGBTQ+ services
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a nonprofit that provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community. The event serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a nonprofit organization that provides crucial services including substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated with unity, joy, and happiness and feel safe.

For performers like Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with helping turn his life around, saying he is three years sober and now can perform on stage as a drag king, something he would not have been able to do without the organization. Weinberger said a significant part of the community, especially gender diverse people, do not have health insurance or funds to access treatment otherwise. The fundraiser is more important than ever, as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. Jack Cesivon, an LGBTQ+ community member, said Transpire Help has helped people who literally have nobody.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed as demand far exceeds $2 million in funds
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month, but applications fill within hours of opening each month.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department oversees an Emergency Rental Assistance Program with nearly $2 million in combined grant funding, but demand far exceeds available resources each month. Program director Dr. James Green told WPTV that the county typically receives about 600 applications within the first couple of hours the portal opens. According to county data combined with 211 information, nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance come in monthly, with approximately 800 applications currently waiting to be processed. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was closed due to overwhelming demand. Green urged anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

The rental market in Palm Beach County has become increasingly unaffordable for residents. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom apartment is $2,020 per month. Joanne Bromfield, who relocated to West Palm Beach from Tampa, spent 12 years as an educator before switching to real estate to earn a higher income, yet continues to worry about making rent almost every day. Twenty-seven-year-old Chellizabeth Colon sought assistance after separating from her husband and became unable to work due to serious pregnancy complications. Green attributed the surge in applications to rising costs of housing, gas, and food. For those unable to access the county program, 211 provides 24/7 connections to nonprofits and other assistance programs throughout the region.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 30 in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties
hero.teaser: Residents will be prohibited from using fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns and landscaping during the rainy season to reduce nutrient runoff that can cause harmful algae blooms.
hero.body:
Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties will implement a fertilizer ban beginning June 30 that prohibits any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen. Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the ban is to help reduce nutrient rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms. Those blooms could disrupt waterways like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River.

"It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs said. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health." Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said a good alternative during the ban is using composting for gardens and landscaping. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape."

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island at Peck Lake, state report warns
cards.teaser: Nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with ocean waters threatening to breach the island at Peck Lake, according to a 2025 state report.
cards.body:
The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could transform a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could disrupt ecosystems dependent on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater. "We're going to probably have more storm surges that would create more of these breaks," Perry said. "That makes all these coastal marshes and everything vulnerable."

At risk are the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, and wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St. Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry noted there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town completed a major beach renourishment project in April 2025, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The town spends about $3 million in taxpayer dollars annually on beach renourishment. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said, warning that a breach could require massive state and federal investment to prevent "cataclysmic erosion."

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections after finding live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in their SpaghettiOs. According to the complaint, the incident occurred in June 2024 when Hubbard purchased the product at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications from consuming the contaminated food.

Attorneys for Hubbard stated she "discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food." The complaint notes that "Hubbard documented the contamination in multiple videos, which clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product." The lawsuit alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product and seeks $50,000 in damages. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance overwhelmed with nearly 8,000 monthly calls for help
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple of hours each month, with nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, but demand vastly exceeds available resources. Program director Dr. James Green told WPTV that the department receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly and currently has about 800 applications in queue. "We typically receive about 600 applications the first couple of hours they're open," Green said. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Anyone in need can call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check availability.

The surge in applications reflects rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, switched careers from a 12-year career as an educator to real estate to afford rent. "Almost every day, all the bills are rising except our paychecks," she said. For those unable to access the county's program, 211 offers 24/7 assistance connecting residents with nonprofits and other area programs. Green urged people with extra housing to partner with the county to help prevent homelessness.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach hosts Pride on the Block as Transpire Help faces funding cuts
cards.teaser: The largest fundraiser for Transpire Help brought together the LGBTQ+ community in West Palm Beach as the non-profit faces government funding cuts that have slashed services in half.
cards.body:
Pride on the Block brought together the LGBTQ+ community and allies at The Peach in West Palm Beach on Saturday for the largest fundraiser supporting Transpire Help. The non-profit organization provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Founder Donna Weinberger said the event creates a celebratory space for attendees. "People can come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe," Weinberger said.

Government funding cuts have made the fundraiser increasingly critical. Weinberger said the cuts have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. "A big part of our community and especially gender diverse folk do not have health insurance or funds so they wouldn't be able to access treatment," Weinberger said. Performer Liam Chambers, who is three years sober, credited Transpire Help with turning his life around. "I can get on the stage, I'm a drag king and I wouldn't have been able to do it without them," Chambers said. Jack Cesivon said the organization's impact is undeniable. "I've seen the differences in my own life and in people all around me. I mean Transpire has helped people that literally have nobody," Cesivon said.

Campbell is urging senators to delay action and involve all stakeholders in shaping new rules.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties face combined $223 million loss under property tax referendum
cards.body:
Three Treasure Coast counties would experience significant revenue losses if voters approve a property tax referendum scheduled for November. According to a study from the Florida Association of Counties, Martin County faces an estimated $50 million loss in 2027-28, growing to $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County projects a $32 million loss in 2027-28, increasing to $57 million in 2028-29. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, reducing property tax bills for homeowners. The savings for homeowners can vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars, depending on the county, city, and assessed value of a home.

Republican lawmakers, including Governor Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, supports the measure as providing relief to working families. "This is more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet," Overdorf said. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell explained that county leadership is working with the Office of Management and Budget to understand the consequences. Officials are considering various options to address potential budget gaps, including finding new revenue sources and implementing budget reductions. "We don't know if it will be an increase in sales tax, we don't know if it will be an increase in user fees for other services, we don't know right now," Powell said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club with 36 members
hero.body:
Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, founded a new junior chess club to introduce his community to the game he loves. The club has already attracted more than 36 young members and meets every Friday in Port St. Lucie. Baptiste's passion for chess started at age 5 when he began playing with his family. Now he wants to share that enthusiasm with other children and draw attention away from technology toward classic board games. "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff," Baptiste said. "I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games."

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess offers significant benefits to young players. She sees the game as a tool for developing important life skills in the next generation of leaders. "It will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making," Kempton said. The club welcomes players at all skill levels, from complete beginners to more experienced players, creating an inclusive environment where children can learn and grow together.

Parents have responded positively to the new chess club. Thomas Furlong, whose children joined the program, described it as an ideal opportunity for his family. He sees the club as a chance for his daughter to learn chess from the beginning while his son can continue improving his skills. The friendly competition between siblings adds another benefit to their participation. Francesca Furlong, one of the club's newest members and a child at the club, enjoys the social aspect most. "I like playing with other kids," she said.

The Atlantis Chess Club continues to expand beyond its original Port St. Lucie location. In addition to its Friday meetings in Port St. Lucie, the club plans to launch two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. This growth reflects the community's enthusiasm for Baptiste's vision of promoting chess among young people. For Baptiste, the mission remains simple and clear. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," he said. The club provides a structured setting where young players can develop strategic thinking skills while forming meaningful connections across Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire reaches 125 acres, now 99% contained after weekend escalation
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown grew from 37.8 acres to approximately 125 acres over the weekend before being brought under near-total control.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard on Friday, June 5, just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the initial blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while MCFR's drone team identified remaining hotspots and confirmed full containment.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire in the same general area. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from MCFR, FFS, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area, though officials confirmed there was no broader threat to the public. The fire reached approximately 125 acres total and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. The Florida Forest Service remains on scene monitoring conditions, with the investigation into the fire's origin ongoing.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block fundraiser aids Transpire Help after funding cuts
cards.teaser: The celebration in West Palm Beach serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, which has seen the number of people it can help cut in half due to government funding cuts.
cards.body:
Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community at The Peach in West Palm Beach on Saturday. The event serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides crucial services including substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated. "People can come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe," Weinberger said.

For performers like Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with helping turn his life around. "I am three years sober and now I can get on the stage, I'm a drag king and I wouldn't have been able to do it without them," Chambers said. The fundraiser is more important than ever, as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. Weinberger noted that a big part of the community and especially gender diverse folk do not have health insurance or funds to access treatment. Jack Cesivon, an LGBTQ+ community member, said Transpire has helped people that literally have nobody.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice the musical closes final performances this weekend at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, featuring actor Ryan Stajmiger in the iconic striped suit.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical is now playing at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7. The Broadway hit brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film.

The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble. Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. Very early in the run, he experienced one unexpected moment when a wig change on stage went wrong. The second wig came off with the first wig, so he was bald for an entire scene.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: 80-mile ocean paddle from Bahamas to Lake Worth Beach to raise funds for cystic fibrosis families
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Event founder Travis Suit said participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. All proceeds benefit the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit established to honor his daughter, Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants will take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner. Friday features a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night.

Safety requirements include a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. All paddlers must wear GPS trackers provided by the event and keep them active throughout the journey, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000, while crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Suit created the event after learning about the natural respiratory benefits of ocean salt air. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to celebrate the paddlers' arrival. For more information, visit crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

hero.headline: Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat Jared Moskowitz Team Up to Urge Floridians to Prepare for Hurricane Season
hero.body:
Republicans and Democrats Unite on Hurricane Preparedness

Florida's hurricane season runs through November, and two congressmen are putting aside partisan differences to encourage residents to get ready. Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican from Congressional District 19 in Southwest Florida, and Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat from Congressional District 23 in Southeast Florida, have created a public service announcement to help Floridians prepare for potential storms. The effort demonstrates that disaster preparedness is a concern that unites people across political lines.

Both lawmakers emphasized that hurricanes pose risks to all Floridians regardless of their political affiliation. "Protecting Florida communities is a shared duty that transcends any political divide," Donalds said, adding that the safety of all Floridians must come first. He encouraged residents to take steps now rather than waiting for a storm to approach. Moskowitz reinforced this message, stating that hurricanes do not discriminate based on party affiliation. "Hurricanes don't care whether you're a Democrat or a Republican; they hit everyone," Moskowitz said. He stressed the importance of beginning preparations immediately instead of waiting until a storm appears on the radar.

The congressmen have outlined specific preparation steps for residents to follow. Floridians should assemble a disaster supply kit containing at least seven days of supplies as soon as possible. Residents need to identify their evacuation zones and understand the distinction between hurricane watches and warnings. Pet owners should develop plans for their animals during emergencies, and business owners should establish emergency procedures for their operations during storm events. Both lawmakers also recommend downloading mobile applications from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to stay informed and connected during hurricane season.

This bipartisan initiative comes as Florida enters an active portion of hurricane season. Donalds is currently running for Florida Governor in this year's elections. Moskowitz announced his candidacy in late May for Florida's 25th House seat, adjusting his campaign focus after the Florida Legislature finalized new redistricting congressional maps in the spring. Despite their different political parties and campaign goals, both representatives have prioritized public safety by working together on this important messaging campaign.

cards.headline: Five Officers Inducted Into Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame in Tallahassee Ceremony
cards.teaser: Representative Kat Cammack presented American flags to five inductees and families at the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame ceremony on Saturday in Tallahassee.
cards.body:
North Florida Representative Kat Cammack presided over induction ceremonies for the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame on Saturday in Tallahassee, presenting American flags to five inductees: Larry Corgin, Michael "Mick" McHale, the late O.L. Raulerson, the late Harrel Reid, and Daniel Slaughter. Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Mark Glass joined Cammack during the ceremony. The inductees brought distinguished careers in Florida law enforcement. Corgin is the retired Assistant Chief in the South Miami Police Department who served for nearly 40 years and volunteered to support police in New York City in the days following the September 2001 terrorist attacks. McHale is a retired Sergeant with the Sarasota Police Department who serves as President of the National Association of Police organizations. Raulerson was the only person elected as sheriff in two different Florida counties, holding office in Highlands and Okeechobee counties across a four-decade career.

Reid served as Sheriff of Hamilton County for nine consecutive terms, making him the longest serving sheriff in state history during his 36 years in office. Slaughter is the retired Chief of the Clearwater Police Department, where he had a 30-year career and helped develop the Real-Time Operations Center, noted as a model for mental health response in law enforcement. Founded by the state Legislature in 2014, the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame honors police and deputies who serve the state. Officers are nominated by the Florida Sheriffs Association, Florida Police Chiefs Association, Florida Police Benevolent Association, Fraternal Order of Police, and the State Law Enforcement Chiefs Association. The Governor and Cabinet vote to approve nominees.

cards.headline: Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert Formally Launches Congressional Campaign for District 24
cards.teaser: Oliver Gilbert III will officially launch his campaign for Florida's 24th Congressional District on Sunday at Antioch Missionary Baptist Church in Miami Gardens, setting up a Democratic primary collision with state Senator Shevrin Jones.
cards.body:
Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert III formally launches his campaign for Florida's 24th Congressional District on Sunday at 10 a.m. at Antioch Missionary Baptist Church in Miami Gardens, where he was born, raised, and twice elected Mayor. The campaign event caps a week in which Gilbert resigned his county seat, filed his Statement of Candidacy with the Federal Election Commission, and launched a campaign site. Gilbert, 53, led Miami Gardens as Mayor from 2012 to 2020 before winning a Miami-Dade Commission seat in District 1, where he served as Commission Chair from 2022 to 2024. A Florida A&M University graduate with a law degree from the University of Miami, he resigned from the Commission effective January 3, the day a new member of Congress would be sworn in.

Gilbert enters the race following Congresswoman Frederica Wilson's announcement that she would not seek a ninth term after eight terms in Congress. The redraw kept Congressional District 24 deeply blue, one of just four Democratic-leaning seats left in the state, making the August 18 Democratic Primary effectively decisive. Gilbert faces competition from former Miami-Dade Commissioner Jean Monestime, physician Rudy Moise, business owner Christine Sanon-Jules, Republican Patricia Gonzalez, and independent Andy Daro. State Senator Shevrin Jones, 42, a Miami Gardens native and 14-year legislative veteran, is preliminarily viewed as the early front-runner. The qualifying deadline is June 12.

cards.headline: Jay Collins Challenges Byron Donalds to Debate in Florida Governor's Race as Fundraising Deadline Approaches
cards.teaser: Retired Green Beret and former state Senator Jay Collins appeared on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures to challenge Congressional District 19 Representative Byron Donalds to a debate in the Republican gubernatorial primary.
cards.body:
Jay Collins, a retired Green Beret and former state Senator, appeared on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures to challenge front-runner Byron Donalds to debate in the Republican gubernatorial nomination race. Collins acknowledged the difficult position he faces in the field and argued that Donalds cannot avoid direct engagement. "You can't hide in the shadows. You can't pull a Biden and hide in a corner behind your couch in the basement. You've got to come out and debate," Collins said. He questioned what Donalds feared if he held such a commanding lead and emphasized that Florida voters should not coronate candidates without competition.

The debate dispute has intensified following the Democratic field's consolidation after Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings withdrew for health reasons, leaving former Congressman David Jolly as the presumptive nominee. Donalds argues Republicans should unite behind him rather than waste resources on internal conflict. However, Collins faces significant resource constraints as he pursues a debate strategy. Donalds has raised approximately $81 million during his campaign, while Collins had raised roughly $1.75 million through the end of March. Fundraising reports covering activity through May are due June 10, a critical deadline as Collins and former House Speaker Paul Renner, who had raised more than $6 million through March, attempt to narrow the financial gap.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds Campaigns on Affordability in Palm Coast After Democratic Field Reshuffles
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds brought his Defending the Florida Dream tour to Flagler County on Saturday, campaigning on affordability a day after Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings suspended his campaign.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds brought his Defending the Florida Dream tour to Palm Coast on Saturday, focusing on affordability issues as the Democratic gubernatorial field reshuffled. Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings suspended his campaign Friday following a prostate cancer diagnosis, leaving former Representative David Jolly as the presumptive Democratic nominee. Donalds declared that the general election starts today with Demings' announcement. On the trail, Donalds worked his affordability message, pledging to cut regulatory burdens he blames for pushing prices higher. "Across the state, Floridians are telling me the same thing: they want Florida to remain Florida," Donalds said. "I'm fighting everyday to make sure everyone has a shot at living the Florida Dream." Campaign Press Secretary Skylar Swanson described the Palm Coast turnout as large and energetic, calling it a sign of momentum.

Donalds, who has raised $81 million, said he would rather spend in the General Election than the Primary now that Democrats have a presumptive nominee. He cites his endorsement from President Donald Trump and a lead of more than 40 points in multiple public polls, saying he will take his message to voters through town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and door knocking rather than debate. With more than two months until the August 18 Primary, his remaining rivals Jay Collins and Paul Renner both insist on debates. Fundraising reports through May are due June 10.

cards.headline: Lauren Book Clears Democratic Primary Field for Florida Senate District 30 as Dan Daley Exits Race
cards.teaser: Former Senate Democratic Leader Lauren Book appears headed for an uncontested Democratic primary after Dan Daley announced Tuesday he would not run for Senate District 30.
cards.body:
Lauren Book, who served in the Florida Senate from 2016 to 2024 before term limits forced her out, has cleared the Democratic Primary field for Senate District 30 after Dan Daley announced Tuesday he would not run. Book announced her campaign after outgoing Senator Tina Polsky confirmed she would not seek re-election. With Daley's exit, Book now has an uncontested path to the Democratic nomination. Qualifying begins this week and closes June 12, with Republican Jerusa Zitta remaining the only other active candidate in the race. The final stretch of qualifying could still produce surprises, as candidates who spent months considering a race may make it official, others who appeared committed may quietly pass, or someone could emerge to file at the last moment.

Book has remained active in her advocacy work, walking 1,500 miles this year for her annual Walk in My Shoes event. With Florida's third Special Session of the year now completed, the state is turning to election season in earnest. This week represents another milestone on the road to November elections.

cards.headline: University of South Florida President Moez Limayem Navigates Series of Campus Tragedies in First Months
cards.teaser: Moez Limayem became the University of South Florida's ninth President on February 17 and has spent his first 3.5 months navigating a catalog of institutional crises with visible personal engagement.
cards.body:
University of South Florida President Moez Limayem has navigated a series of institutional crises during his first 108 days in office since becoming the university's ninth President on February 17. In mid-April, doctoral students Nahida Bristy and Zamil Limon, both 27-year-old Bangladeshi students, disappeared from the Tampa area. Limon's roommate, Hisham Abugharbieh, was arrested and charged with two counts of first-degree murder, with prosecutors seeking the death penalty. Limayem spoke at a public vigil, was visibly emotional, and told the community he understood the loss as a former international student and father. He promised a comprehensive review of off-campus housing safety and committed USF to stop recommending complexes that did not meet standards. This week, the university announced a new off-campus housing provider program in direct response.

Just days after Bristy's remains were identified, the Marine Science Laboratory at USF's St. Petersburg campus caught fire, with more than 200 firefighters responding. The 80-year-old building housing the College of Marine Science's chemistry, biology, and oceanography research operations was declared a total loss. Limayem ran his first commencement ceremonies in early May with two empty chairs on the arena floor during the doctoral ceremony representing Bristy and Limon, who both received degrees posthumously. On May 17, 21-year-old honors student Lauryn Akey was killed on Interstate 75 in Charlotte County when an alleged drunk driver made a wrong-way turn. This week, 21-year-old student Hansel Pearson stabbed his roommate and another person at Halo 46 Apartments near campus before being found dead hours later.

hero.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres, now 99% contained after weekend escalation
hero.body:
A brush fire that started Friday in Indiantown spiraled out of control over the weekend before firefighters brought it under near-total control by Sunday morning. The fire eventually consumed approximately 125 acres and reached 99% containment as of Sunday, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service.

The incident began on Friday, June 5, when Martin County Fire Rescue responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Firefighters quickly contained the initial blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to prevent the flames from spreading further. Martin County Fire Rescue also deployed its drone team to identify remaining hotspots and confirm full containment before crews left the scene. Though the cause remained unknown at the time, early indications pointed to a holdover fire, in which a lightning strike could have smoldered underground for days before igniting visible flames. The Florida Forest Service has continued investigating the fire's origin.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation deteriorated dramatically when crews returned to the same area to fight a much larger 120-acre brush fire. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds combined with dense vegetation fueled rapid fire growth, triggering a large-scale response that included Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Forest Service, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters focused on protecting nearby structures as smoke blanketed the surrounding area. Officials confirmed there was no broader threat to the public, though residents were warned to expect smoky conditions throughout the weekend as suppression efforts continued.

By Sunday morning, firefighters had achieved 99% containment of the fire, which reached a total size of approximately 125 acres. The Florida Forest Service remained on scene monitoring conditions to prevent any additional flare-ups. Authorities said the investigation into the fire's origin remains ongoing.

His daughter Francesca, one of the club's newest members, said the best part of joining is "playing with other kids."

cards.headline: Palm Beach County parents and commissioner respond to teen takeover trend at Wellington mall
cards.teaser: A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase law enforcement presence at the mall.
cards.body:
A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase law enforcement presence on Friday. Shoppers noticed the heightened police presence, including parent Savanna Restrepo, who was picking up her son Isaac from summer camp. Restrepo said she had seen posts circulating online about the event ahead of time and found the visible police presence reassuring. Fellow parent Eric Delgado also supported the law enforcement response, saying "We need a strong police presence."

Teen takeovers are large gatherings of teens at malls, beaches or parks that typically devolve into violence. The trend has been spreading across Florida, including an event in Clearwater at the end of May that resulted in widespread property damage, fights and the shooting of a 17-year-old. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier called the events "unacceptable" and announced a plan to investigate and prosecute those responsible. Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss said community safety is a priority while also addressing the root cause. He noted that kids need activities to fill their time and pointed to community rec centers offering programming throughout the day. Weiss acknowledged that summer camp costs can be a barrier for families and said Palm Beach County offers scholarship opportunities for summer camps.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County woman accused of stealing $60,000 from bingo hall
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County woman faces charges for allegedly stealing $60,000 from a bingo hall.

A woman from St. Lucie County has been accused of stealing $60,000 from a bingo hall. The alleged theft was reported Saturday.

The woman faces charges related to the theft of the substantial sum from the bingo hall. The investigation was conducted by local law enforcement.

Details about the alleged theft were reported by WPBF. The case remains under investigation by authorities in St. Lucie County.

cards.headline: Masked intruder arrested after Port St. Lucie apartment break-in, $300 watch stolen
cards.teaser: A masked intruder was arrested following a break-in at a Port St. Lucie apartment where a $300 watch was stolen.
cards.body:
A masked intruder has been arrested after breaking into a Port St. Lucie apartment and stealing a $300 watch. The break-in occurred Saturday.

The suspect wore a mask during the apartment intrusion in Port St. Lucie. Police arrested the intruder following the incident.

The stolen item was a watch valued at $300. Video of the arrest was reported by cw34.com.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor accused of abusing 5 foster children at her home
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces accusations of abusing five foster children who lived in her home.
cards.body:
A pastor in Fort Pierce has been accused of abusing five foster children at her home. The accusations were reported Sunday.

The pastor allegedly abused the five foster children who were placed in her care. The children lived at her Fort Pierce residence.

The case involves multiple foster children who were under the pastor's care. WPBF reported the accusations against the Fort Pierce pastor.

cards.headline: Red Cross assists families after fires in Fort Pierce and other areas
cards.teaser: The Red Cross is helping families affected by fires in Fort Pierce, Loxahatchee Groves and Boynton Beach.
cards.body:
The Red Cross is providing assistance to families affected by fires in Fort Pierce, Loxahatchee Groves and Boynton Beach. The fires occurred over the weekend.

Families in Fort Pierce were among those receiving Red Cross support following the fires. The organization also aided families in Loxahatchee Groves and Boynton Beach.

The Red Cross response covered multiple locations across the region. WPBF reported on the assistance efforts for the fire-affected families.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club
cards.teaser: Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, has launched a new juniors chess club to share his love of the game with the community.
cards.body:
A new juniors chess club has launched in Port St. Lucie, inspired by 9-year-old Orion Jean Baptiste, who wanted to share his love of the game with his community. Baptiste's passion for chess began at age 5, playing alongside family members. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said. He hopes to pass that passion on to others, noting that many young people focus on technology instead of board games. "I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games," Baptiste said.

More than 36 juniors have already joined the Atlantis Chess Club, which meets at Port St. Lucie every Friday. The club will soon begin two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess will help develop the next generation. "It will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making," Kempton said. The club attracts players of all skill levels. Thomas Furlong brought his children to join, and his daughter Francesca Furlong, one of the newest members, said she likes playing with other kids.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration at Palm Beach State College
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration, marking a milestone for foster youth served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
cards.body:
35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. ChildNet supports foster kids and young men and women through education, adoptions and independent living resources.

Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward. Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber. Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the significance of the evening, saying "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard."

cards.headline: Palm Beach County parents and commissioner respond to teen takeover trend at Wellington mall
cards.teaser: A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to step in with increased law enforcement presence.
cards.body:
A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase law enforcement presence. The event drew responses from parents and county officials concerned about preventing future incidents. Teen takeovers are large gatherings of teens at malls, beaches or parks that typically devolve into violence. The trend has been spreading across Florida, including an event in Clearwater at the end of May that resulted in widespread property damage, fights and the shooting of a 17-year-old.

Shoppers at the Wellington Green Mall on Friday noticed the heightened police presence. Savanna Restrepo, who was there picking up her son Isaac from summer camp, said the visible police presence was reassuring. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier called the events "unacceptable" on social media and announced a plan to investigate and prosecute those responsible. Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss said community safety is a priority but pointed to parental involvement as a root cause. He noted that Palm Beach County offers community rec centers with programming throughout the day and scholarship opportunities for summer camps, urging parents to know what their kids are doing and stay in contact with them.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block fills West Palm Beach with celebration for LGBTQ+ community
cards.teaser: A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community.
cards.body:
A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community. The event serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides crucial services including substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated, allowing people to "come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe."

For performers like Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with helping turn his life around, saying he is three years sober and can now perform on stage as a drag king, something he would not have been able to do without the organization. Weinberger emphasized that the fundraiser is more important than ever, as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. A big part of the community, especially gender diverse folk, do not have health insurance or funds to access treatment, she said.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres over weekend, now 99% contained
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue an.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service. The incident started on Friday, June 5, when MCFR firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened at the time. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while MCFR's drone team identified remaining hotspots and confirmed full containment before crews cleared the area.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to the same general area to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident, with shifting winds and dense vegetation contributing to rapid fire growth. The large-scale response involved MCFR, the Florida Forest Service, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office working to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area. The fire reached approximately 125 acres in total size and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. Officials noted the fire's cause was unknown, though early indications suggested it may have been a holdover fire from a lightning strike that smoldered underground before igniting visible flames. The Florida Forest Service remains in the area monitoring conditions while authorities continue investigating the fire's origin.
